name: Church & Dwight Co., Inc.
moat_justification: A portfolio of #1/#2 niche brands (ARM & HAMMER, OxiClean, Trojan, TheraBreath, Hero) with decades of shelf presence, proven pricing power, and a repeatable acquisition playbook, run asset-light — but the categories are low-switching-cost staples where shelf space is rented from powerful retailers, larger rivals can out-promote, category growth is ~3%, and the $357.1M VMS impairment in 2024 proved acquired brands can decay. Moderate-strong, not wide.
fragility_flags: STALE_FY: latest fiscal year ended 9 months ago — check TTM/quarterly OE and consider --base-oe-ps override
NI_OCF_DIVERGENCE: net income and operating cash flow differ by >40% in 2024 — find the one-off (tax deposits, impairments, WC swings) before trusting the OE base
WIDE_SCENARIO_SPREAD: super-bull IV is 4.8x super-bear IV — uncertainty is huge; confidence should not be high
one_liner: High-quality staples compounder, moat 6/10 — at $104.63 the weighted IRR is only 7.94% (IV@15 $43.71); it clears 15% only at or below $43.71.
moat_for: #1/#2 niche positions — ARM & HAMMER cat litter 24.5% share, TheraBreath #2 mouthwash at 25.3%
Proven pricing power — Q2 2026 price/mix +1.5% while holding laundry share vs P&G/Henkel promo wave
Decades-old brand equity with national distribution and growing e-commerce
Repeatable acquisition playbook — TheraBreath, Hero, Touchland scaled internationally
Asset-light cash conversion — capex ~2% of sales, OE positive 5 of last 5 years
moat_against: Near-zero switching costs and private-label exposure in commoditized categories
Retailer power — shelf space is rented, not owned
Larger rivals (P&G, Henkel, Colgate) with deeper promo/marketing budgets
Slow category growth (~3% weighted average) caps the organic runway
Brand durability not guaranteed — $357.1M VMS impairment 2024 and 2025 business exits
Growth depends on continued acquisitions at full prices
